item.title: I ditched Google for SearXNG, and going back feels like a downgrade
item.itunes:title: I ditched Google for SearXNG, and going back feels like a downgrade
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
You probably don't give a lot of thought to the search engine you use. After all, Google dominates the market in such a way that no one ever considers the alternatives. But as useful as they are, search engines like Google (and even its competitors) collect data about you and your queries, and use them to serve ads or present results that are either sponsored or benefit the companies financially.

There are more user-focused alternatives like DuckDuckGo, but if you truly want to own your search experience, SearXNG is the way to go. I recently started using it instead of Google, and I already can't imagine going back to the old way of doing it.

SearXNG is so much cleaner

Just give me the results I want

If you've used Google in recent years, you're probably already aware of how the search UI has become cluttered with a wide range of things you or may not care about. It used to be just about search results, but now, you get an AI overview first and foremost, and before that there were things like widgets for images, definitions, questions and answers, and so on. They can be useful, but they can get in the way of what used to be a very straightforward experience.

SearXNG brings things back to a simpler UI that gives me what I'm looking for and keeps me in control. When I search for something, it returns all the results as a list of URLs; some of them may include thumbnails, but it's still just a standard list, though in some cases, you may see an "info" panel If I want images, I can switch to the appropriate tab for them, and in fact, there are tabs for other big categories, including news, social media, and specific topics like IT and science (though I find these two odd as dedicated categories).

Should you use a self-hosted search engine?

What are the options and benefits in self-hosting a search engine?

1
By  Tom Li

But SearXNG isn't a search engine in itself, it's a metasearch engine. It takes your queries and sends them to all major search engines, stripping them of private data that could be used to identify you, plus the service itself stores no personally identifiable information. And when you make a search, each search result is labeled with the search engine(s) that returned said result, which can also help you identify the more useful engines to you.

I have full control over the experience

I can choose the search engines

What's really cool about SearXNG is that it puts me in full control over the search experience. The search results are clearly categorized, but I can also change the search engines used by SearXNG. The service strips data out of your queries, but if you don't want Google to get your queries at all, you can just disable it through SearXNG's preferences.

The available search engine options by default are already very solid, including Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, and Qwant for general searches, Wikipedia, translation engines such as dictzone and lingva, and much more for all different kinds of results. To clarify, I deployed SearXNG using the Proxmox helper script.

You can choose which search engines can show results in general searches, but even if you disable them, you can also search for specific queries using a prefix. For example, if you want to search for a specific quote on Wikiquotes, you can use the prefix !wq before your search, and it will only return results from that search engine, making it easy to narrow down results to the kind of information you want. This works even if you've disabled that search engine, so it's very versatile.

In total, there are 260 search engines already built into SearXNG, though you won't see as many out of the box. You can add more of the supported engines by modifying the settings.yml file inside the container. You can even add private search engines by using an access token, though this isn't something I tried to do.

This self-hosted search engine uses Google, but still protects your privacy

The ease of Google Search with less tracking and no ads

By  Megan Ellis

You don't have to self-host

There are multiple public instances

As great as it is to have your own private search engine, self-hosting your own services may not be for everyone. If you're not willing to jump through that kind of hoop, you can actually use SearXNG through a wide range of public instances. The SearXNG team even has an official list of public instances you can access without any work on your side, which makes things much easier.

Public instances still allow you to tweak your preferences for searching, since those are saved in your browser, meaning each user has their own settings. What's different is you can't edit the settings.yml file since that's stored on the server, which also means you may have different engines available by default compared to deploying your own container from scratch. This may make things easier if you don't want to mess around with the terminal, but it can also limit your options.

I don’t pay for Perplexity or ChatGPT after combining my local LLMs with Perplexica and SearXNG

It's a neat way to avoid outdated responses to my queries

5
By  Ayush Pande

There's a downside to that, which is that, of course, your search queries are then being sent to a third-party server, which may undermine some of the benefits you're using SearXNG for. Still, it may be easier to trust a relatively small server that isn't ad-supported than a company like Google.

SearXNG is fantastic

Before this, I hadn't really considered the possibility of using a self-hosted search engine, but SearXNG quickly proved itself to me. It can bring me results from all the search engines in a cleaner interface, filter results to specific engines, and give me full control over the search experience. I love how capable it is, and Google certainly feels less mine in comparison.

item.title: TORRAS’ OSTAND Q3 Series offers the iPhone 18 Pro lineup rugged protection
item.itunes:title: TORRAS’ OSTAND Q3 Series offers the iPhone 18 Pro lineup rugged protection
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Phones are everywhere. Those small rectangles are basically computers in your pocket. And most of us don’t go anywhere (or do anything) without one. They’re high-precision pieces of futuristic technology that integrate into basically every part of our daily lives. Since they’re handled so often, it’s only a matter of time until they encounter a fall.

Most of us have dropped our phones at least a few times. That’s why they need armor.

But most cases are too bulky, don’t do what they’re supposed to, or are built like bricks. Thankfully, TORRAS (the company behind the TORRAS Airbag phone case series) has found a way to offer your phone the right amount of protection without restrictions or design flaws. So it’s no surprise that the TORRAS Ostand Q3 Series has well-engineered features that keep your iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max safe.

TORRAS Ostand Q Series: Two cases that stand up and stand out

The TORRAS Q3 Series has two unique cases: the TORRAS Ostand Q3 Rugged and the TORRAS Ostand Q3 Air Pro. Each case is built to precise standards that ensure maximum protection. They have plenty of useful features you won’t find in many other cases. They are meant to look good, be comfortable to grip, and, most importantly, protect your phone’s components.

Each case in the collection is different, but there are standard features that unite them. The TORRAS Q3 Series cases have a 3-in-1 ring called the TORRAS Ostand. It’s a kickstand, hanging point, and magnetic mounting platform all in one. The handy feature has three modes: Stand, Hang, and Snap.

In Stand Mode, you can use your case as a kickstand, which works great if you need to set up a recording or want to comfortably watch a video. The ring itself can rotate 360 degrees horizontally and opens up 180 degrees vertically. This stand can also be locked (and it’ll remain stable) during use.

In Hang Mode, you can quite literally hang your phone on something. If you’re hiking, running, or working out, you can loop it onto anything to keep it stable and safe while it’s in use.

Snap Mode is where this feature really shines. There are Halbach-arrayed N54 magnets with 18N (Newtons) of magnetic force for attachments. Most things that stick tend to stay that way. The connection is strong and secure enough to handle a magnetic car mount, chargers, bike mounts, and plenty of other accessories. It’s a great asset for a bumpy ride or trip.

Design-wise, these cases also have heavily engineered airbags on the top and bottom, an .08mm camera lift, and a 1.2 mm screen guard, as well as a soft lining inside. And if that’s not enough, all of the TORRAS Ostand Q3 Series cases come with a modern stylus, so you get great protection and added functionality, too.

The TORRAS Ostand Q3 Air Pro’s Air Duet™ technology provides optimum cushioning

TORRAS Ostand Q3 Air Pro for iPhone 18 Pro
Weight
53g
Screen protector included
No

TORRAS' Ostand Q3 Air Pro offers just enough protection in its slim, lightweight build, offering Air Duet™ airbag technology to keep your iPhone protected from impact and a grippy texture to keep your phone firmly in hand. There's even a handy kickstand to make hands-free viewing simple.

See at TORRAS

If you’re looking for a sleek, well-engineered case that can handle your active lifestyle, the Q3 Air Pro is a good mix of lightweight design and heavy-duty construction. The case features incredible Air Duet™ airbag technology, with engineered air chambers at the top and bottom to protect your device. It’s meant for everyday use and is ideal for long hikes and just spending time exploring the Great Outdoors. It’s light too, weighing only 53g.

On top of the dual-layer airbag construction, the Q3 Air Pro has a protective outer layer with anti-slip texturing and a soft microfiber lining inside. The outer layer acts as a shallow chamber, while the inner layer is flexible. When your iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max is dropped, the outer layer essentially “takes the hit” while the inner layer disperses the shock away from the device.

Credit: Torras

The case looks great, too, with several color schemes available. Violet Summit offers a vibrant purple tone, while Polar Slate is a calming blend of cool, contrasting blues. Alpine Marble offers a modern gunmetal look, while Obsidian Core’s black and gray color scheme gives a futuristic feel.

The TORRAS Ostand Q3 Rugged offers easy handling on your bumpiest adventures

TORRAS Ostand Q3 Rugged for iPhone 18 Pro
Screen protector included
No

When extreme durability is a priority, the TORRAS Ostand Q3 Rugged is the case to take you on your next adventure. It is constructed with longevity in mind, boasting a polycarbonate plate and Air Cushion technology. Best of all, you get the extra protection without a whole lot of heft. This case also has the Ostand for added versatility.

See at TORRAS

If you seek adventure and need something a bit more rugged, the TORRAS Ostand Q3 is built to keep the iPhone 18 Pro Series safe. The case uses a polycarbonate plate in its construction, which makes it solid enough to protect your phone but light enough to hold and use comfortably.

It might look like a traditional rugged phone case on the surface, but it’s much more than that. To begin with, it’s not as bulky as a typical rugged case. The modern design has clean lines and a streamlined look. The side of the base has textured slide rails (with a rock-inspired look) that make gripping the phone easy.

In terms of protection, instead of using the Air Duet airbag structure, Ostand Q3 Rugged uses Air Cushion technology. It’s engineered to withstand repeated impacts, similar to what most users might experience every day. And the magnetic grip on the included TORRAS Ostand means you can attach chargers, mounts, wallets, and other accessories easily.

Credit: Torras

This is the type of case you’d use if you go on lengthy bike rides often or do a lot of outdoor exploration. This model can also be helpful if you work in less forgiving occupations like construction or manufacturing, or for those who tend to be on the clumsy side. With a rugged, durable case, you have a lot less to worry about.

The case comes in several fantastic color schemes as well. Sunrise Silver and Jet Black offer sleek, modern designs while Plum Purple and Island Blue liven up the case’s look.

A durable phone case for any occasion

Whether you’re looking for a lightweight kickstand case or something with a bit more sturdiness, TORRAS has quality phone cases that don’t trade safety for functionality; this includes the Ostand Q3 Series cases for the iPhone 18 Pro Series. With this kind of durability and precision, you can worry less about damaging your phone and focus more on living life instead.

Brought to you by TORRAS

item.title: I replaced the Windows clipboard with Snipboard, and it fixed every problem I had with it
item.itunes:title: I replaced the Windows clipboard with Snipboard, and it fixed every problem I had with it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The Windows clipboard is an essential tool, but it's one that has felt somewhat neglected throughout the years. Windows 10 finally gave us a clipboard history, but that feature hasn't evolved significantly since its initial debut. And while some rivals exist, they also tend to feel either outdated or clunky.

Snipboard is aiming to change that, and it does so extremely well. Joining the growing family of productivity and customization apps from Stardock, this may be one of my favorites yet, making the clipboard feel faster and more useful than ever.

About this article: Stardock provided XDA with early access and a license for the Snipboard beta release. The company had no input on — nor an early preview of — its content.

Clipboard history as it should be

Fast, responsive, and persistent

As useful as the clipboard history is on Windows 11, it's also severely flawed in a few ways. The biggest, to me, is the lack of a search capability in the UI, along with the fact that clipboard items aren't retained across reboots unless you pin them. I would also say that the UI in general doesn't feel as fast as it could be.

Snipboard fixes pretty much all of these issues. It takes over the Windows + V shortcut by default (though it can be remapped), and it appears instantly. You can set it to open on any edge of the screen, or make it appear in a more compact floating design similar to the native Windows solution, but it's always faster. You can browse results with the arrow keys or select an option by pressing Ctrl and any number from 1 to 9, and you can even select formatting options like pasting as plain text or changing the text to uppercase using just the keyboard.

Unlike the official Windows solution, anything saved to your clipboard is kept there until your allotted storage or the set timer (both of which can be customized) runs out, so rebooting your PC doesn't mean you lose access to those items. They're always there, and pinning items just means they're always at the top and never deleted to save space.

6 clipboard managers for Windows that will change how you work

The clipboard is more than you might think

10
By  João Carrasqueira

To make it easier to sift through long lists of copied items, once you've summoned the clipboard, you can start typing to search for items in your clipboard — though I've noticed that some keys, like V and B, don't seem to automatically trigger the search. Alternatively, pressing the up arrow lets you filter items, which includes selecting the search option so you can type freely. It's not quite perfect yet, but it's a huge improvement from what Windows offers.

On top of all this, Snipboard doesn't just work with text or images. In addition to those two types of items, it can also save copied items like files and folders in File Explorer. These items also persist across reboots, so you can always bring them back up later.

It syncs across devices

No cloud needed

What makes Snipboard even better is that it's not just a clipboard history for one PC, but it's also an engine for keeping those copied items synced across multiple PCs. Microsoft does offer something similar, but while that solution uses the cloud and can sometimes be slow, Stardock's syncing works entirely within your home network, so data is never sent outside your home.

Syncing works by creating a link code on one of your devices and entering it in another, which enables items to stay in sync between those two devices. It's not clear how the licensing will work for the standalone version of Snipboard, but the current version is included at no additional cost in Object Desktop, and that supports up to five devices, so you can get a fairly big network of synced devices right out of the gate.

Sync is customizable, too, so you can choose whether synced items are automatically downloaded to each device or if they should only be downloaded when selected from Snipboard (the default behavior). This isn't a huge deal for text or small images, but if you're copying files, it can make a big difference, and it effectively lets you move files from one PC to another very easily. You can also choose whether pinned items should be kept in sync across devices.

One thing I will point out is that there is no sort of buffer method, so if you copy an item on one PC while the other PC isn't on, that clipboard item won't sync, even if the two PCs are online at the same time at a later point.

This free and open-source self-hosted app syncs your clipboard across all of your devices

Say goodbye to the hassle of transferring text

5
By  Anurag Singh

You can tweak its looks, too

It wouldn't be a Stardock app otherwise

Stardock apps usually lean heavily on customization, and Snipboard is no different. Some of the options are more functional, like changing the position of the dock or the behaviors for syncing. One thing I touched on is that you can also change how long clipboard items are saved (the default is to keep them forever) and the size of the clipboard history, which is set to 1GB by default. This determines how many files are kept until older ones need to start being deleted.

But much of the customization is also visual. The app comes with an array of preset color themes, but you can also customize the individual colors for each app element and tweak things like the thickness of the highlight outline or set a transparency level for the background, so you can let your desktop background shine through.

It's not the usual, almost overwhelming, level of control Stardock apps often have, but I'd say that's a good thing in this case. There's no need to go overboard for something this simple, and there's already plenty of customization to be had here.

Hands-on: Fences 6 makes your desktop even more efficient

Organize your desktop like never before

2
By  João Carrasqueira

Snipboard is great

Even though it's still in beta, Snipboard makes the Windows clipboard exactly what I'd want it to be. It's faster, more capable, and more useful than the built-in solution, on top of offering polenty of customization options and a very welcome sync engine.

During the beta period, Snipboard is included at no additional cost in Stardock's Object Desktop suite, so it's a total no-brainer if you're already subscribed. We don't know how much the standalone release will cost yet since it's not planned to release for a while, but that will be a big factor in whether it's worth it or not. In the meantime, you can also try the app for free for 30 days to see if it's worth it to you.

Snipboard

Windows 10/11

Stardock

item.title: I turned off one Pixel feature and gained hours of battery life
item.itunes:title: I turned off one Pixel feature and gained hours of battery life
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My Pixel 8’s battery life was never terrible, but some days the drain didn’t make sense. I could leave the phone sitting on my desk, barely touch it for an hour, and still watch the battery percentage drop faster than expected.

Eventually, I realized the problem wasn’t an app running wild in the background. It was the cellular connection. That is when I changed one network setting, and it ended up making a much bigger difference to my Pixel’s endurance than I expected.

I fixed my Pixel's Bluetooth issues by changing this one setting

I wish I had known about unrestricted Bluetooth access for accessories years ago.

12
By  Patrick O'Rourke

My Pixel was draining battery while doing nothing

Weak 5G coverage was the real problem

The strange part about my Pixel 8’s battery drain was that I didn’t even need to use the phone for it to happen. At first, I went through the usual suspects, such as background apps and syncing, but eventually started paying attention to the cellular signal.

That turned out to be the bigger problem. 5G coverage around my home isn’t strong, and my Pixel would often struggle to maintain a solid connection. Instead of simply sitting on a stable network, it could keep searching for a better signal or bouncing between 5G and LTE.

That matters because a cellular modem has to work harder when reception is poor, which increases power consumption even when I am barely touching the phone. Once I realized that, keeping 5G enabled all day started making very little sense.

Most Pixel devices also use Samsung’s Exynos modem, and cellular efficiency has historically been one of the weaker areas compared with phones using Qualcomm modem platforms.

I switched my Pixel to LTE only

Standby drain improved the most

Once I figured out that weak 5G coverage was contributing to the drain, I stopped trying to make 5G work and switched my Pixel to LTE only. I headed to Settings -> Network & internet -> SIMs -> Preferred network type -> LTE.

It was a small change, but the difference was noticeable. Instead of jumping between 5G and 4G or hanging onto a weak 5G signal, my phone now stays on a much more consistent LTE connection. It may not look as impressive on a spec sheet or in a speed test, but for how I use my phone outside, it is more than fast enough.

The biggest improvement, though, has been the standby drain. Before making the switch, I could leave my Pixel sitting idle and still watch the battery percentage drop faster than I expected. With LTE enabled instead, idle drain feels much more controlled and predictable.

Before this change, I averaged around three and a half hours of screen-on time whenever I was mostly on a cellular network. With this tweak, I managed to extend that by at least an hour.

item.title: I changed one Samsung setting and my phone finally stopped draining overnight
item.itunes:title: I changed one Samsung setting and my phone finally stopped draining overnight
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Losing a little battery overnight is normal, but waking up to find my Samsung phone down by nearly 10-12% every morning started to feel ridiculous. I wasn’t scrolling, streaming, gaming, or even touching the phone, yet plenty was still happening behind the scenes.

Instead of tweaking (and restoring them again in the morning), I automated how my Galaxy behaves while I sleep. I set up one Samsung Routine that automatically shuts down unnecessary activity at night and brings everything back to normal by morning.

Android Auto kept disconnecting until I changed one hidden setting

The solution to my issue was more straightforward than I expected.

41
By  Patrick O'Rourke

My phone was losing nearly 10-12% overnight

That’s a lot

My biggest frustration was seeing my Galaxy S25 Ultra battery drop by nearly 10% overnight, even though I wasn’t using the phone at all. I would go to bed with plenty of charge left, leave my Galaxy untouched for seven or eight hours, and still wake up to a noticeable chunk of battery missing.

That might not sound dramatic on paper, but it started affecting my mornings more than I expected. If I had forgotten to charge the night before, I would wake up already thinking about topping up the phone before heading out.

On busier days, that meant plugging it in while getting ready or carrying a charger just to be safe. The drain also felt wasteful because most of it was happening while the phone was sitting idle.

Background apps, notifications, syncing, and other overnight activity were still doing their thing when I needed almost none of it. That is when I decided to automate the entire nighttime setup instead.

I stopped hunting for individual battery hogs

Samsung Routines became the fix

At first, I approached the problem the obvious way: I started looking for individual apps that might be responsible for the overnight drain. I checked the battery usage, restricted a few apps, and kept wondering whether some rogue service was waking my phone in the background.

That is when I stopped chasing individual battery hogs and turned to Samsung Routines instead. Rather than micromanaging every app, I created one routine that tells my Galaxy to calm down while I am asleep.

Setting it up is straightforward. I opened Settings -> Modes and Routines -> Routines, created a new Routine, and used a specific time period as the trigger. Mine runs automatically from 2 AM to 9 AM, which covers the hours when I am normally asleep.

You don’t have to use a fixed schedule, either. You can pair the Routine with Samsung’s Sleep mode, or create a widget on the home screen and trigger it manually whenever you head to bed.

Then comes the fun part: choosing what actually happens during those hours. I have my routine turn off the always-on display, enable power saving, and close apps running in the background. These are all things I don’t need while I am sleeping, so keeping them active makes little sense to me.

You can take the setup much further, though. Depending on how aggressive you want to be. You can tweak the performance profile, turn off Wi-Fi, disable mobile data, and more. I personally prefer keeping these enabled.

The best part is that everything reverses automatically

The overnight drain finally became predictable

The best part about this setup is that I never have to undo anything in the morning. Once the Routine ends at 9 AM, my Galaxy automatically returns to its normal behavior. The always-on display comes back, power saving switches off, and the phone is ready for my usual daytime workload without me having to set or remember which toggles I changed the night before.

That automation is what made the whole thing stick for me. I have tried plenty of battery-saving tricks in the past, but most of them depended on me remembering to enable something before bed and reverse it the next morning.

Eventually, I would forget. With Routines, the entire process happens quietly in the background.

More importantly, my overnight battery drain has become far more predictable. Instead of waking up to a drop of around 10%, I now usually lose roughly 2% overnight. That is a much more manageable number, and no longer throws off my morning.

I turned off one Samsung feature and gained hours of battery life

My Samsung suddenly lasted much longer.

3
By  Parth Shah

My phone finally survives the night

This sleep Routine fixed one very specific problem for me, but that is exactly why I like Samsung Routines so much. I can build them around the small annoyances that show up in my own day. I can build automations for driving, charging, working, gaming, traveling, or practically any part of my day.

That is what makes Routines so useful: you decide the trigger, choose exactly what your Galaxy should do, and then forget about it. So don’t copy my setup and call it a day. Get creative, experiment with different combinations, and build Routines around your own habits.

item.title: Your motherboard still has a reset button for a password almost nobody sets anymore
item.itunes:title: Your motherboard still has a reset button for a password almost nobody sets anymore
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
You might have a Windows password on your PC, but I'm pretty sure you don't have one for your BIOS/UEFI. There was a time, though, when password-protecting your BIOS was nothing unusual. PC users simply had a "supervisor" password on their systems in addition to any other safeguards in place.

The more surprising part of the story is that your modern motherboard still has a way to reset the UEFI password. Manufacturers can't remove the functionality just because no one uses a BIOS password anymore. The CLR_CMOS jumper is still a part of motherboards to prevent hard locks and help IT staff manage fleets of machines.

5 problems you didn't know a CMOS reset could fix

Resetting the CMOS can resolve issues such as black screens, a bad overclock, or an undervolt tweak, as well as stability problems.

7
By  Abhinav Raj

I remember when BIOS passwords were a thing

Yes, I'm 34 years old

It must have been during the 2000s when my parents were fond of locking the home computer with a Windows password. This top-tier security method was necessary to prevent my brother (fellow XDA writer Samarveer Singh) and I couldn't waste hours playing games. When we figured out how to remove any Windows password they set, my father pivoted to the BIOS password — we couldn't even get to the boot stage anymore.

Setting a supervisor/administrator password in the firmware prevented unauthorized users from messing with the settings. It used to be a decent line of security when disk encryption or OS-level login security hadn't matured. It increased the hassle by forcing you to enter two passwords instead of one, but the benefits were clear. When people figured out how to wipe the BIOS password with a couple of motherboard pins, however, it stopped being so secure.

I finally updated my BIOS — don't wait as long as I did

BIOS updates are nothing to be afraid of; you'd only gain something most of the time

7
By  Tanveer Singh

A motherboard jumper wipes the password, along with the BIOS settings

It sounds surprisingly simple

The method I'm referring to is the CLR_CMOS jumper — a pair of pins usually near the bottom edge of the motherboard. Bridging or shorting these pins with a piece of metal, such as a screwdriver, for 10 to 15 seconds once your PC is unplugged reverts your BIOS/UEFI to factory defaults. Your motherboard may have this jumper labeled JBAT, CLRTC, RTCRST, or CLR_BIOS.

I've used this jumper to revert to stable BIOS settings after an adventurous overclock or when facing a boot loop after a BIOS update. I've never done it on a modern system, hence, I didn't get the chance to use a motherboard switch or rear I/O button to reset the BIOS. Although PC users rarely set the BIOS password anymore, there's no incentive to remove this reset method — it's just a couple of pins on the board.

Besides, it still helps people fix weird system bugs and recover from issues that are too time-consuming to diagnose. When a 15-second BIOS reset brings your system back to stable settings, why waste hours diagnosing the underlying problem? It only sounds lazy if the issue comes back. Those buying older systems with supervisor passwords or IT admins managing multiple machines know the importance of the CLR_CMOS jumper.

This 20-year-old Windows tool fixed my dead PC when nothing else would

Even if you have no other recovery USB, make sure you have this one

3
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Not every machine resets the BIOS password with a simple jumper

Added security prevents unauthorized access

The CLR_CMOS jumper doesn't universally wipe your BIOS settings. Anyone with physical access to your PC can easily use it to remove the BIOS password and access your PC's firmware settings. To avoid this in enterprise environments, organizations use server motherboards that store firmware passwords in NVRAM (non-volatile RAM). Modern laptops almost always do the same using non-volatile EEPROM, flash memory, or TPM chip.

Other systems require a specific key sequence to reset the BIOS password, bolstering the system security. The CLR_CMOS jumper method works for your home computer, but it won't be effective on a laptop, business machine, or server hardware.

Your PC's firmware has a hidden storage limit, and it can stop your computer from booting

The smallest drive in your PC is the one you've never checked.

By  Korbin Brown

BIOS passwords are obsolete, but we still need the reset switch

Almost nobody locks their BIOS with a password anymore, but the CLR_CMOS functionality is still needed on modern motherboards. Whether you remove your motherboard's battery, use a physical switch, or short a pair of pins, you need a way to clear the BIOS settings to recover from a failed boot or unexplained system behavior.

item.title: I turned my old Android phone into the ultimate universal TV remote
item.itunes:title: I turned my old Android phone into the ultimate universal TV remote
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I didn't set out to replace the remotes for my TV setup, but I was tired of digging through the couch cushions every time I couldn't find them. My old Android phone already pulls its weight as a backup media server when needed, and since it stays mostly in the living room, I thought of doubling it up as a universal TV remote.

With a couple of apps and about twenty minutes of experimenting, I turned my old Android phone into the best universal TV remote I've ever owned. It also made my coffee table free from remotes.

Google TV makes Android phones surprisingly good remotes

The official remote app is all you need for Google TV devices

While other apps are available, the Google TV app makes it easy to use an Android phone as a TV remote. It works on both Android TV and Google TV devices, and it doesn't require any additional hardware elements like an IR blaster. Setting it up is also straightforward. You just connect the phone and TV to the same Wi-Fi network; once that's done, the app can search for and pair with compatible TVs nearby.

Google TV app
See at Google Play Store

As for the app itself, Google TV offers basic controls, including volume, navigation, and playback. It can also bring up the keyboard when required, which is particularly useful as it's much easier to type on the virtual keyboard than with the remote.

Another benefit of the Google TV app is that it's compatible with iOS, and it works just as well on an iPhone as on an Android phone. However, this remote app will only work if your TV supports Google's remote functionality.

Third-party apps expand compatibility beyond Google TV

An old Android phone can still be used to control smart TVs running different OS

Google's official app works well, but it can't control every smart TV, which is where third-party apps come in. Many of these apps support LG TVs running webOS, Samsung smart TVs running Tizen OS, and TCL models running Roku OS or Fire OS. Some work with TVs that are from non-mainstream companies.

Among the ones I tried, Universal TV Remote for All TV from BoostVision is full of ads, and while Any TV Remote Control from Klebo doesn't bombard you with ads, it puts some important features behind a subscription package. For instance, the on-screen isn't available on the free version.

iRemote from TechSmart Group is a decent pick, but it relies heavily on ads if you don't buy the subscription, and it lacks a keyboard. UniMote from SkippyLab is the best of the ones I have tested so far. It doesn't have full-screen ads, supports swipe navigation, brings keyboard support without any subscription, and lets you quickly launch apps.

UniMote remote TV app
See at Google Play Store

At the core, most of these apps work in the same way as Google's solution. That is, as long as the phone and the TV are on the same network, these apps can control the TV over Wi-Fi.

My old Android phone became the ultimate universal TV remote with its IR blaster

An IR blaster lets your phone control almost any TV

To turn my old Android phone into a truly universal TV remote, I used its built-in IR blaster. It turns the phone into a traditional infrared remote, and the smartphone and TV don't need to stay on the same Wi-Fi network. A fair number of apps support this setup as well, but my old Android phone already came with its own pre-installed IR remote app. It has a big limitation, though.

The app has no keyboard implementation that can take advantage of the infrared sensor, and I couldn't find a third-party app that does either. On the bright side, the IR remote app has all the essential controls and can send commands for volume, channel, and input changes.

One phone can replace a pile of remotes

An old Android phone can live a second life by being a universal TV remote

The remote situation in my TV setup became much simpler after I turned my old Android phone into a universal remote. However, this might not apply to everyone, since not all Android phones have a built-in IR blaster. Third-party apps that rely on Wi-Fi make things easy, but many require subscriptions or include aggressive ads.

Even with these limitations, the Android phone can serve as a proper backup TV remote when needed.

The future of Android-powered TV streaming sticks looks uncertain

The Google TV Streamer was released in 2024 and the future of something new isn't clear.

4

item.title: Docker containers can fail without crashing, and this one setting catches them before your users do
item.itunes:title: Docker containers can fail without crashing, and this one setting catches them before your users do
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Docker Compose made it easy to spin up my whole self-hosted stack with one file and one command. But what it didn’t do was tell me whether any of those containers were actually working or had crashed. I’d only find out something was broken when the web app became inaccessible or I saw database connection errors. By then, I’d already lost time chasing the problem. Adding a handful of extra lines to my compose file helped me change that. I no longer have to wait to run into issues since Docker tells me when something’s off.

Forget about Portainer, I use this simple tool to manage all my Docker containers on my NAS

I use Dockge to manage all my Docker containers, and I won't look back (except in some instances).

7
By  Adam Conway

A running container stack isn’t always a working one

I found broken containers only when I went looking for them

The only way I knew something was wrong with a container was when I experienced the issue myself. And when I did, I’d open a terminal window, run docker ps command, and see a table of containers that were marked as Up. I’d assume all was fine. But then I’d reload the web app, clear the cache, and still get nothing. No error, just a blank page.

Half of the time, the container itself was running just fine. The actual problem was buried somewhere else. The main service had locked up, or the app lost its connection to the database. As far as Docker was concerned, nothing was wrong.

I followed the same fix: restart the container and get on with my day. But what actually got me was the lack of clarity about what went wrong until I ran into the problem myself. It caught me off guard, and I went to use the same app that had quietly stopped responding an hour earlier.

Health checks tell Docker what working means

A single block to report every container’s status individually

Playing detective across a bunch of containers can get tiring fast. And I wanted to build my home lab, not troubleshoot it forever. I started adding the health check block into my compose files. With that block, Docker runs the command on schedule to report whether the container is healthy or unhealthy. Docker marks it as unhealthy if the command fails or times out.

The only catch with health checks is that Docker runs the command inside the container itself. So I had to make sure the image actually had curl or wget installed. Databases needed a different set of tools: Postgres uses pg_isready, and Redis uses redis-cli ping to report their health status.

I really found the start_period parameter helpful the hard way, all thanks to containers like Nextcloud and Immich. For containers that take a while to boot, Docker was flagging them as unhealthy before they’d even finished starting. By adding a grace period to the health check routine, Docker stopped marking them unhealthy prematurely. That’s where a restart policy comes in, but it only goes so far.

Adding restart policies only covered crashes

Fixing problems for anything that’s supposed to run 24/7

For the services running round the clock, this gap in Docker’s reporting actually matters. For example, Netdata is only useful for monitoring my network if it’s actually running. Same goes for my media server’s availability. I’d rather have Docker raise a flag and send me a notification than have someone in my house tell me Jellyfin is unreachable.

I used the restart policy, but it only kicks in when a container exits. So if the web app is non-responsive, the container is still deemed alive. Since the process is running, Docker does nothing regardless of the health check. The restart policy made me look closely at how Docker handles a container that is frozen but still reported as running.

The default unless-stopped option works for most things. To make Docker restart an actually unhealthy container, I use another helper container called autoheal. It watches container status and acts on it. I point Uptime Kuma at my services and get a notification the moment something flips.

Uptime Kuma
Key highlights
Open-source monitor

Uptime Kuma is a lightweight, easy-to-use monitoring tool that offers multiple ways to keep you up-to-date about the status of your self-hosted services

See at Github

Making apps start after other components are ready

Setting resource limits helps manage the physical resources

Dealing with containers that have separate database components is trickier than I expected. Earlier, the web app started without waiting for the database to be ready. That caused several containers to fail on boot. My Docker Compose file would spin up the database part first and wouldn’t wait for it to accept connections. That often left me confused with errors about failure to connect or crashing. With a simple condition called service_healthy, the app container waits until Postgres actually reports healthy before it attempts to start. That alone saved me several confusing troubleshooting sessions.

For heavy containers that run all the time, setting resource limits allows me to accommodate other containers and experiments comfortably. Just like Portainer and other management interfaces offer sliders, I can set the CPU and memory usage limits for each container. Setting resource limits also keeps components from getting unnecessarily stressed, especially by heavy containers that run 24/7.

5 Docker Compose tricks that made my home server more reliable

A collection of tips and tricks that leveled up my Docker Compose game

By  Ayush Pande

Start with health checks and build everything around them

When I started with Docker Compose, I skipped health checks to get containers running faster. That was a wrong call. Once a container knows its own health, everything else falls into place. Docker Compose respects the startup order, restart policies, and hands off status to external monitoring tools like Uptime Kuma. A few lines in the compose file do all of that heavy lifting.

If you’re already organizing your Compose files or keeping secrets out of your config, health checks belong to the same sitting. Add those health check blocks first, and the rest of the stack behaves the way you expect.

Docker

Docker Desktop is a one-click-install application for your Mac, Linux, or Windows environment that lets you build, share, and run containerized applications and microservices. It provides a straightforward GUI (Graphical User Interface) that lets you manage your containers, applications, and images directly from your machine.
Docker Desktop reduces the time spent on complex setups so you can focus on writing code. It takes care of port mappings, file system concerns, and other default settings, and is regularly updated with bug fixes and security updates.

See at Docker

By  Adam Conway

A running container stack isn’t always a working one

I found broken containers only when I went looking for them

The only way I knew something was wrong with a container was when I experienced the issue myself. And when I did, I’d open a terminal window, run docker ps command, and see a table of containers that were marked as Up. I’d assume all was fine. But then I’d reload the web app, clear the cache, and still get nothing. No error, just a blank page.

Half of the time, the container itself was running just fine. The actual problem was buried somewhere else. The main service had locked up, or the app lost its connection to the database. As far as Docker was concerned, nothing was wrong.

I followed the same fix: restart the container and get on with my day. But what actually got me was the lack of clarity about what went wrong until I ran into the problem myself. It caught me off guard, and I went to use the same app that had quietly stopped responding an hour earlier.

Health checks tell Docker what working means

A single block to report every container’s status individually

Playing detective across a bunch of containers can get tiring fast. And I wanted to build my home lab, not troubleshoot it forever. I started adding the health check block into my compose files. The only catch with health checks is that Docker runs the command inside the container itself. So I had to make sure the image actually had curl or wget installed. Databases needed a different set of tools: Postgres uses pg_isready, and Redis uses redis-cli ping to report their health status.

I really found the start_period parameter helpful the hard way, all thanks to containers like Nextcloud and Immich. For containers that take a while to boot, Docker was flagging them as unhealthy before they’d even finished starting. By adding a grace period to the health check routine, Docker stopped marking them unhealthy prematurely. That’s where a restart policy comes in, but it only goes so far.

For the services running round the clock, this gap in Docker’s reporting actually matters. For example, Netdata is only useful for monitoring my network if it’s actually running. Uptime Kuma
Key highlights
Open-source monitor

Uptime Kuma is a lightweight, easy-to-use monitoring tool that offers multiple ways to keep you up-to-date about the status of your self-hosted services

See at Github

Dealing with containers that have separate database components is trickier than I expected. Earlier, the web app started without waiting for the database to be ready. item.title: I built a recovery USB that can fix a Windows PC even when Windows won't boot
item.itunes:title: I built a recovery USB that can fix a Windows PC even when Windows won't boot
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Getting locked out of your OS and being thrown into a boot loop is one of the biggest fears when it comes to personal computing, and when we're talking about Microsoft Windows, there are quite a number of ways you can end up in that awkward place. Maybe it was a bad update, a power-loss event mid-write, or a corrupted boot record. No matter the reason, this specific problem hurts everyone the same.

In my 23 years of using Microsoft Windows, I've run into this issue a handful of times, and that's enough to realize that it's better to be prepared for this happenstance than to dread it. So I took a 64GB USB flash drive that sat in the drawer doing nothing and turned it into a recovery kit. Here's everything I've got on it, and why.

Ventoy comes first, for obvious reasons

Install, drag, and drop

Everything on my recovery USB drive runs through Ventoy, and I'd argue there's no better tool for it. It's free, and once it's installed, you can copy ISO files onto the USB like any other file. You can boot from it, and Ventoy lists everything you've added, which means there's no need to dedicate a separate flash drive for your "rescue" tools and the OS image.

I've set mine up with GPT and Secure Boot support enabled, and then sorted the ISOs into numbered folders, so the boot menu stays organized. Even though I've got four ISOs on the drive, it still has more than 40GB of storage free, which is terribly resource-efficient.

The official Windows 11 ISO

Microsoft offers this for free

Not a lot of people know that it's possible to download the Windows 11 ISO from Microsoft directly instead of going through the process of creating a Windows 11 installation media. I like to keep that ISO on the drive because it doubles as a Windows recovery tool as well.

You can boot into it from the Ventoy menu, pick your language, and click "Repair your computer" on the setup screen instead of clicking "Install now." That opens the Windows Recovery Environment, which happens to be the same one Windows loads on its own after a persistent boot loop. This copy, however, does not depend on anything stored on the broken drive.

Hiren's BootCD PE

A working Windows desktop when yours won't load

Hiren's BootCD PE is a free Windows Pre-installation Environment for Windows 11. There's a very specific problem this one solves, so bear with me as I explain this. Windows' own recovery tools exist to repair the OS, but they give you a menu and a Command Prompt, not a computer that you can use.

This utility, on the other hand, boots into a familiar desktop environment and loads drivers for graphics, sound, Wi-Fi and Ethernet on its own, so you can have a working network connection for further troubleshooting or working. This gives me a chance to browse the internal drive, copy files to safety, and even check the disk for errors. When the repair options in the Windows ISO fail and a clean reinstall is the only way forward, this is how I can get my files off the drive before wiping it altogether.

Rescuezilla

For a full, clean backup

Like everything on the list, this one's also a free utility with a simple GUI. Rescuezilla is an imaging tool that can back up an entire drive to an image, restore the said image, or clone one drive to another, and its images are compatible with Clonezilla. Before attempting any repair that writes to the disk at all, I'd image the drive first, so that even a failed fix can be rolled back.

SystemRescue

For any damage below the file level

Credit: SystemRescue.

Anyone who has ried to recover a Windows drive has probably faced this issue at somepoint, wherein booting into a recovery tool and opening the drive list doesn't list one of your storage drives. Sometimes, it shows up as RAW, and Windows asks you if you want to format it before using it. When this would happen to me, I'd just try to make peace with the fact that my files are probably gone. What I learnt later, however, is that the data can still be on the disk, and it's the partition table or file system that's damaged, which the Windows ISO and utilities like Hiren can't fix.

SystemRescue is worth a try should you run into an issue like this. It's a Linux distro that's purpose-built to solve this problem. TestDisk can find the missing partition most times and write it back, and GParted can check it once it's visible again. If the drive is failing physically, ddrescue can copy whatever it can still read to another disk and skip bad sectors instead of stalling on them the way a normal file copy does. Worth mentioning that its built-in Memtest also lets me rule out issues with the system memory.

Never let your machine reach a place where your mind hasn't reached first.

Remember to try the usual fixes first!

All these tools are nice to have on your emergency recovery drive, and can serve you well if you find yourself in an unfortunate position with your OS. When it comes to system recovery, I subscribe to a simple rule derived from aviation, which is to never let your machine reach a place where your mind hasn't reached first.

Before you reach for the recovery drive, though, always remember to try the usual fixes, which include unplugging any new peripherals you've been trying out, resetting the CMOS, or letting Windows attempt its own Quick Machine Recovery. Plenty of boot problems are usually resolved through this route.
